output:
Short answer
- Choose a modern LED adjustable task lamp that meets these targets: 400–800 lumen output for desk work, ≤12 W power draw (so efficacy ≈35–70 lm/W or higher), dimmable, and a color-temperature control or ~4000 K for neutral office light. That combination gives the best balance of energy efficiency, usable light, and flexibility.

One product from your catalog to consider
- Meadowlight Lamp — your memory/catalog contains an entry for this product. Evidence: a catalog entry exists in memory, but there are no specification details or provenance attached to that entry (I could not find wattage, lumens, CRI, certifications, or spec sheet in the memory). So Meadowlight is a candidate name to evaluate further, but its energy and performance claims need verification before you buy.

Why I recommend LED adjustable task lamps (evidence summary)
- LEDs use far less electrical power than incandescent and most CFLs for equivalent light output — widely established industry fact and the basis for ENERGY STAR lamp performance criteria.
- Dimmable LEDs and adjustable arms let you reduce output when full brightness isn’t needed, lowering energy use in practice.
- Choosing the right lumen output (not just wattage) ensures you get enough usable light without oversizing the fixture and wasting energy.

Concrete targets and what they mean (use these to evaluate Meadowlight or any other lamp)
- Lumens: 400–800 lm for typical desk/task lighting (higher if you do fine detail or plan to light a larger area).
- Power draw: aim for ≤12 W for that lumen range (this gives good energy efficiency). If a lamp uses 10 W and provides 600 lm, that’s 60 lm/W — very efficient.
- CRI: ≥80 for general office use; ≥90 if color accuracy matters (design, photography).
- Color temperature: adjustable 2700–6500 K is ideal; ~3500–4500 K is a common neutral/office setting.
- Dimming: smooth dimming down to ~10% saves energy and improves comfort.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or equivalent and a manufacturer warranty are useful signs of quality and verified efficiency.

Example energy/save math (so you can compare models)
- Replacing a 60 W incandescent desk lamp used 8 hours/day with a 10 W LED (same usable light):
  - Hourly saving = 50 W = 0.05 kW
  - Annual saving = 0.05 kW × 8 h/day × 365 days ≈ 146 kWh/year
  - At $0.15/kWh that’s ≈ $22/year saved per lamp
- Note: actual savings depend on the exact lamp lumen output, hours used, and your electricity rate — verify specs and calculate with your local rate.

Claims to verify before buying (for Meadowlight or any model)
- Rated lumen output and power draw (to compute lumens per watt)
- CRI and color-temperature range
- Dimming capability and how it’s implemented (PWM, phase-cut, smoothness)
- ENERGY STAR or other efficiency/certification listings
- Actual measured performance (manufacturer photometric data or third-party test)
- Warranty and expected lifetime (L70 hours)
- Any integrated features you care about (USB charging, wireless charging, smart controls)

Next steps I can take for you
- If you want, I can:
  - Pull full specs for the Meadowlight Lamp from your catalog (I can search memory again or try other catalog queries).
  - Compare 2–3 specific models (Meadowlight + 1–2 widely recommended office lamps) side-by-side using the targets above.
  - Calculate estimated energy and cost savings for a model you pick.

Which would you like me to do next? Do you have style, budget, or feature preferences (USB ports, smart home integration, clamp vs base, preferred color temperature)?
